item.title: For women and children in West Africa, medical treatment often came too late. Then one model changed where care begins.
item.description:
The medicines already existed. The challenge was reaching people in time. Muso’s model of proactive community healthcare is showing what becomes possible when care moves closer to families.

In 2009, a community health worker in the bustling capital of Bamako, Mali, found a young boy at home who had become dangerously ill within a matter of hours. Recognizing he needed urgent medical care, she arranged for him to be taken to a health facility.

The journey was five kilometers, but distance was only part of the challenge. The boy’s father carried him on foot, then into an ambulance, then back on foot to cross a river, then into another ambulance.

“At that time, it was very difficult for the ambulance to move within the community, because there were no clear roads,” says Djoumé Diakité, MD, co-founder and Mali Country Director of Muso, a nonprofit that had launched its Rapid Care approach the year before to address poor health outcomes in the region.

At the clinic, a handful of doctors and nurses were responsible for everything from prenatal care to emergency medicine. The boy had severe malaria-related anemia and needed a blood transfusion. “It was very difficult to have access to blood at the facility,” Diakité says. “I gave my own blood [to replenish the supply].”

The boy spent 10 days in the clinic — a sacrifice his family could scarcely afford. Ten days at his bedside meant 10 days without work or wages for his father. Saving the boy’s life also meant feeding the parent caring for him.

“That story touched my heart deeply — I imagine myself in that [situation], choosing between feeding [my] family and bringing one of them to the [health clinic],” Diakité says.

He and the community health worker (CHW) who found the boy know exactly what would have happened had she not reached him when she did.

For decades, the global fight against child mortality focused on building hospitals, funding medical breakthroughs, and expanding formal health systems. Yet in places like Mali, one of the most powerful tools for saving children’s lives was hiding in plain sight: CHWs — mostly women — already living among the families they served, trusted by their neighbors but largely overlooked, underfunded, and excluded from the center of health policy.

Muso set out to change that.

The system’s blind spot

When Muso launched Rapid Care in 2008, about one in seven children in Mali died before their fifth birthday. The medicines to save many of them already existed; the problem was access. In Bamako’s poorest neighborhoods, five kilometers could feel like fifty. And even families who reached a clinic often faced another barrier: Since 1984, national law had required patients to contribute to the cost of their own care, giving community health associations the authority to charge fees at every step.

These impossible trade‑offs were playing out in communities across sub-Saharan Africa. Diakité and one of his Muso cofounders Ari Johnson, a physician and global health researcher, saw that healthcare was arriving too late. How could they remove the financial and logistical barriers to preventive and diagnostic services, and reach families before illness became an emergency?

For years, CHWs in countries like Mali and Côte d’Ivoire operated in a policy gap: essential in practice, but unsupported and unrecognized on paper. They delivered care without salaries, legal recognition, or the protections that come with formal workforce status. Globally, women make up about 67 percent of the health and social care workforce, yet they remain disproportionately concentrated in lower-paid and unpaid roles. Women in Global Health estimates that at least 6 million women worldwide work as unpaid or underpaid CHWs. (In Bambara, a lingua franca of Mali, Muso means “woman.”)

CHWs were already right there in Mali’s underserved communities, already familiar to neighbors. Diakité and Johnson advocated for governments to invest in them. Local authorities pushed back.

“They were not confident [that] people who never went to the school of medicine could provide quality care at the household level,” Diakité recalls. “The chief medical officer said to us, ‘If you make a mistake, I will send you to jail.’”

Slow access to care created a vicious cycle. Conditions that could have been treated early became emergencies, overwhelming clinics with preventable cases and stretching scarce resources ever thinner. “Once you lose that first contact and the trust is broken, the whole system [pays] the price,” explains Christian Rusangwa, Muso’s Director of Technical Assistance.

Muso’s leaders understood that empowering CHWs was worth the risk — that reducing child mortality in Mali, and now through Muso-supported programs in Côte d’Ivoire and Zambia, could begin with something as simple as a knock on the door.

The woman everyone calls

In Côte d’Ivoire’s rural Madinani district, that knock on the door often comes from Brigitte Kouadio, a professional CHW who is trained, paid, and supervised through a partnership between Muso and the Ministry of Health through proactive community case management, or ProCCM. On paper, she covers about 107 households; in reality, she is woven into daily life. Kouadio visits homes, listens for symptoms, and decides who she can treat herself and who needs to go to a facility.

One recent afternoon, a young boy named Okore stopped playing and went to bed with a fever. His mother, Diahou Apo Natacha, called Kouadio, who immediately came to the house to examine Okore and perform a rapid malaria test. When the test came back negative and the boy’s condition looked serious, she gave basic care, then arranged transport to the hospital.

“By the grace of God, Muso covered all the costs — we did not pay anything,” Natacha recalls. After three days and a blood transfusion, they returned home. Kouadio visited again to go over the medication and show the family how to give it correctly. Natacha says the CHWs in her village “take very good care of us;” Kouadio says that since that episode, the family has fully embraced her, and they have “become like a second family.”

At first, families didn’t believe that care could really be free, assuming there must be a catch. Only after they saw, again and again, that they truly did not have to pay — whether at home or at the hospital — did they start calling as soon as something was wrong. For families used to losing days in the search of healthcare, Diakite says, it was “like they discovered gold in front of their door.”

Rebuilding the system around community health workers

Behind Natacha’s phone call, there’s now an entire architecture. Since 2008, Muso and the Malian government have worked to co‑develop a model that treats CHWs as the organizing principle; in late 2019, Côte d’Ivoire’s Ministry of Health partnered with Muso to adopt that model into its national health system. Health workers are recruited from within their communities; Muso and government partners train them, equip them with protocols and tools, and pay them a salary. Supervisors visit regularly to review cases, and clinics are staffed and stocked to receive referrals. Care is free at home and in facilities.

By rebuilding trust and bringing care closer to home, the model not only reduces preventable illness and death — it helps stabilize the health system itself, allowing every level of care to function more effectively.

A common thread supporting the initiative’s success: Trust the people closest to the challenges to develop the most effective solutions. This principle extends all the way to the apps and platforms CHWs use to manage cases. “The state-of-the-art digital tools are designed not in Silicon Valley, [but] in Yirimadio, in the Mopti region, in Madinani or Adzopé,” Johnson says. “They’re designed with the CHWs who understand the problems and the best ways to solve them. That’s the key.”

From village fix to national backbone

Muso is now working with Côte d’Ivoire’s Ministry of Health on a legal framework that would give CHWs formal status, stipends, training, and social protection. The government counts about 12,000 CHWs nationwide; over the course of just 15 months, Muso helped extend free care, supportive supervision, and digital tools to 8,000 of them. Through a program known as CMU+, the Ivorian government rolled out free care across 2,823 rural health facilities from May to December 2025, opening access to 13 million eligible people.

Zambia is next. In 2024, the country’s Ministry of Health signed a memorandum of understanding with Muso to adapt the model in a politically stable nation where healthcare is already free nationwide. For Rusangwa, success there would demonstrate that centering CHWs can improve outcomes not only in places grappling with conflict and fragile health systems, but also in stable, peaceful countries — a crucial step toward Muso’s ultimate goal: “to end the child and maternal mortality crises and deliver universal health coverage at scale.”

In Diapé, that ambition looks like a mother reaching for her phone when her child grows hot with fever, and a CHW in a khaki Muso vest walking toward a house where she is welcomed like family. For families on the margins of care, the future does not arrive with a ribbon‑cutting; it knocks on the door.

This article was produced in partnership with Big Think.

The medicines already existed. The challenge was reaching people in time. Muso’s model of proactive community healthcare is showing what becomes possible when care moves closer to families.

In 2009, a community health worker in the bustling capital of Bamako, Mali, found a young boy at home who had become dangerously ill within a matter of hours. Recognizing he needed urgent medical care, she arranged for him to be taken to a health facility.

The journey was five kilometers, but distance was only part of the challenge. The boy’s father carried him on foot, then into an ambulance, then back on foot to cross a river, then into another ambulance.

“At that time, it was very difficult for the ambulance to move within the community, because there were no clear roads,” says Djoumé Diakité, MD, co-founder and Mali Country Director of Muso, a nonprofit that had launched its Rapid Care approach the year before to address poor health outcomes in the region.

At the clinic, a handful of doctors and nurses were responsible for everything from prenatal care to emergency medicine. The boy had severe malaria-related anemia and needed a blood transfusion. “It was very difficult to have access to blood at the facility,” Diakité says. “I gave my own blood [to replenish the supply].”

The boy spent 10 days in the clinic — a sacrifice his family could scarcely afford. Ten days at his bedside meant 10 days without work or wages for his father. Saving the boy’s life also meant feeding the parent caring for him.

“That story touched my heart deeply — I imagine myself in that [situation], choosing between feeding [my] family and bringing one of them to the [health clinic],” Diakité says.

He and the community health worker (CHW) who found the boy know exactly what would have happened had she not reached him when she did.

For decades, the global fight against child mortality focused on building hospitals, funding medical breakthroughs, and expanding formal health systems. Yet in places like Mali, one of the most powerful tools for saving children’s lives was hiding in plain sight: CHWs — mostly women — already living among the families they served, trusted by their neighbors but largely overlooked, underfunded, and excluded from the center of health policy.

Muso set out to change that.

The system’s blind spot

When Muso launched Rapid Care in 2008, about one in seven children in Mali died before their fifth birthday. The medicines to save many of them already existed; the problem was access. In Bamako’s poorest neighborhoods, five kilometers could feel like fifty. And even families who reached a clinic often faced another barrier: Since 1984, national law had required patients to contribute to the cost of their own care, giving community health associations the authority to charge fees at every step.

These impossible trade‑offs were playing out in communities across sub-Saharan Africa. Diakité and one of his Muso cofounders Ari Johnson, a physician and global health researcher, saw that healthcare was arriving too late. How could they remove the financial and logistical barriers to preventive and diagnostic services, and reach families before illness became an emergency?

For years, CHWs in countries like Mali and Côte d’Ivoire operated in a policy gap: essential in practice, but unsupported and unrecognized on paper. They delivered care without salaries, legal recognition, or the protections that come with formal workforce status. Globally, women make up about 67 percent of the health and social care workforce, yet they remain disproportionately concentrated in lower-paid and unpaid roles. Women in Global Health estimates that at least 6 million women worldwide work as unpaid or underpaid CHWs. (In Bambara, a lingua franca of Mali, Muso means “woman.”)

CHWs were already right there in Mali’s underserved communities, already familiar to neighbors. Diakité and Johnson advocated for governments to invest in them. Local authorities pushed back.

“They were not confident [that] people who never went to the school of medicine could provide quality care at the household level,” Diakité recalls. “The chief medical officer said to us, ‘If you make a mistake, I will send you to jail.’”

Slow access to care created a vicious cycle. Conditions that could have been treated early became emergencies, overwhelming clinics with preventable cases and stretching scarce resources ever thinner. “Once you lose that first contact and the trust is broken, the whole system [pays] the price,” explains Christian Rusangwa, Muso’s Director of Technical Assistance.

Muso’s leaders understood that empowering CHWs was worth the risk — that reducing child mortality in Mali, and now through Muso-supported programs in Côte d’Ivoire and Zambia, could begin with something as simple as a knock on the door.

The woman everyone calls

In Côte d’Ivoire’s rural Madinani district, that knock on the door often comes from Brigitte Kouadio, a professional CHW who is trained, paid, and supervised through a partnership between Muso and the Ministry of Health through proactive community case management, or ProCCM. On paper, she covers about 107 households; in reality, she is woven into daily life. Kouadio visits homes, listens for symptoms, and decides who she can treat herself and who needs to go to a facility.

One recent afternoon, a young boy named Okore stopped playing and went to bed with a fever. His mother, Diahou Apo Natacha, called Kouadio, who immediately came to the house to examine Okore and perform a rapid malaria test. When the test came back negative and the boy’s condition looked serious, she gave basic care, then arranged transport to the hospital.

“By the grace of God, Muso covered all the costs — we did not pay anything,” Natacha recalls. After three days and a blood transfusion, they returned home. Kouadio visited again to go over the medication and show the family how to give it correctly. Natacha says the CHWs in her village “take very good care of us;” Kouadio says that since that episode, the family has fully embraced her, and they have “become like a second family.”

At first, families didn’t believe that care could really be free, assuming there must be a catch. Only after they saw, again and again, that they truly did not have to pay — whether at home or at the hospital — did they start calling as soon as something was wrong. For families used to losing days in the search of healthcare, Diakite says, it was “like they discovered gold in front of their door.”

Rebuilding the system around community health workers

Behind Natacha’s phone call, there’s now an entire architecture. Since 2008, Muso and the Malian government have worked to co‑develop a model that treats CHWs as the organizing principle; in late 2019, Côte d’Ivoire’s Ministry of Health partnered with Muso to adopt that model into its national health system. Health workers are recruited from within their communities; Muso and government partners train them, equip them with protocols and tools, and pay them a salary. Supervisors visit regularly to review cases, and clinics are staffed and stocked to receive referrals. Care is free at home and in facilities.

By rebuilding trust and bringing care closer to home, the model not only reduces preventable illness and death — it helps stabilize the health system itself, allowing every level of care to function more effectively.

A common thread supporting the initiative’s success: Trust the people closest to the challenges to develop the most effective solutions. This principle extends all the way to the apps and platforms CHWs use to manage cases. “The state-of-the-art digital tools are designed not in Silicon Valley, [but] in Yirimadio, in the Mopti region, in Madinani or Adzopé,” Johnson says. “They’re designed with the CHWs who understand the problems and the best ways to solve them. That’s the key.”

From village fix to national backbone

Muso is now working with Côte d’Ivoire’s Ministry of Health on a legal framework that would give CHWs formal status, stipends, training, and social protection. The government counts about 12,000 CHWs nationwide; over the course of just 15 months, Muso helped extend free care, supportive supervision, and digital tools to 8,000 of them. Through a program known as CMU+, the Ivorian government rolled out free care across 2,823 rural health facilities from May to December 2025, opening access to 13 million eligible people.

Zambia is next. In 2024, the country’s Ministry of Health signed a memorandum of understanding with Muso to adapt the model in a politically stable nation where healthcare is already free nationwide. For Rusangwa, success there would demonstrate that centering CHWs can improve outcomes not only in places grappling with conflict and fragile health systems, but also in stable, peaceful countries — a crucial step toward Muso’s ultimate goal: “to end the child and maternal mortality crises and deliver universal health coverage at scale.”

In Diapé, that ambition looks like a mother reaching for her phone when her child grows hot with fever, and a CHW in a khaki Muso vest walking toward a house where she is welcomed like family. For families on the margins of care, the future does not arrive with a ribbon‑cutting; it knocks on the door.

This article was produced in partnership with Big Think.

The post For women and children in West Africa, medical treatment often came too late. Then one model changed where care begins. appeared first on Skoll.org.

item.title: 3 winnaars van een Volkswagen ID Buzz Pro Winnaarsverhalen Premium 10 augustus 2026 Geen gouden envelop deze keer, maar wel een hele mooie prijs op 4 wielen. Lees meer
item.description:
Geen gouden envelop deze keer, maar wel een hele mooie prijs op 4 wielen. Op postcode 2411 WC in Bodegraven en 1013 XR in Amsterdam wacht in totaal 3 deelnemers een bijzondere verrassing: een gloednieuwe Volkswagen ID Buzz Pro, dankzij hun Premium lot. Quinty gaat bij ze langs.

maandag 10 augustus 2026 — Winnaarsverhalen, Premium

Een nieuwe tourbus voor Mark 

Quinty gaat eerst langs bij Mark en Maeike in Amsterdam. Buiten wacht hun prijs al: een gloednieuwe Volkswagen ID Buzz Pro. Maeike slaat haar handen voor haar mond als ze de auto ziet. Mark is zanger en kan de prijs heel goed gebruiken: "Ik heb nog een nieuwe auto nodig om naar optredens te gaan!" 

Nieuwe auto, nu nog een chauffeur 

Ook buurvrouw Lamroh wordt opgehaald om haar prijs te bewonderen. Ze staat te trillen op haar benen van blijdschap, al heeft ze zelf geen rijbewijs. "Mijn vriend gaat hier enorm om lachen", zegt ze met een glimlach van oor tot oor. 

Vakantie staat al gepland 

Petra had altijd gehoopt dat de Postcode Loterij ooit bij haar zou aanbellen. Dat het nu echt gebeurt, had ze nooit verwacht: "Ik weet niet wat ik moet zeggen." Haar plan staat al vast: "Ik ga met mijn 2 kinderen op vakantie naar Oostenrijk. Zo'n bus komt dan enorm goed van pas."

item.title: How Indian farmers are improving yields and supporting each other with the help of a free farming hotline
item.description:
For millions of farmers, the difference between a good harvest and a devastating loss can come down to getting the right advice at the right time.

In Odisha, India, a free agricultural helpline is helping farmers with advice based on real-time data—enabling them to act faster when pests, weather, or crop disease threaten their livelihoods. For Sradhanjali Pradhan, one phone call can help save her crops—and once she gets an answer, she shares it with her neighbors.

Her story shows what becomes possible when local leadership, real-time data, and practical technology come together: farmers can protect what they grow, strengthen their incomes, and help entire communities become more resilient.

Hear one farmer’s story

Early in Sradhanjali Pradhan’s farming career, when pests destroyed her crops, she lost more than just the thousands of rupees she was counting on and the food she was growing for her family that season. The crop failure meant she could barely afford to pay her daughter’s school fees.

Today, Pradhan can act quickly—and help many others in her community do the same.

Whenever she spots a damaged flower or suspects a pest infestation in her crops, Pradhan, a farmer in the Indian state of Odisha, has a secret weapon: She pulls out her phone and calls 155333, a free hotline known as the Krushi Samrudhi Helpline (KSH), which is run by the state’s agriculture department. On the other end of the line is a KSH representative who can log her question so an agronomist can respond with timely advice on how to avert crop damage before it’s too late. Thanks to a central database, whoever answers the phone can pull up details about Pradhan’s farm, including its size, the soil type, and the crops she grows.

Once Pradhan learns what to do, she spreads the word to others.

“As soon as I know which treatments to use, I tell the nearby farmers so they don’t need to call for the same disease,” she says. Pradhan takes particular pride in sharing the information with older farmers who aren’t comfortable with mobile technology or those who haven’t yet noticed the threat. Sometimes she receives an inbound call from KSH’s command center, which provides customized advisory information. Either way, Pradhan’s fellow farmers rely on her to stay one step ahead, and with her one phone call, an entire village benefits.

When Pradhan spots crop damage, she calls 155333, a free agriculture helpline run by Odisha’s state agriculture department. 

A representative logs her question, and an agronomist follows up with advice tailored to her farm, crops, soil, and local conditions. 

That guidance helps Pradhan respond before pests or disease spread — and then she shares what she learns with other farmers in her village.

A community of women farmers

Over the past several years, Pradhan has become more than a farmer. She’s now a trusted source of agricultural knowledge for her fellow farmers and a central figure in her community as the secretary of a women’s self-help group (SHG) with members from multiple villages. She is married to a photographer, and they have a daughter.

Pradhan’s day starts with family time: She cooks breakfast and lunch for her husband and daughter and makes sure they have everything they need for work and school. In the early afternoon, once the sun is past its peak, she goes out into the fields. She often works alongside her best friend, Ranjukta Maharana, and other friends whose fields are close by. They chat and catch up as they work the land. “It’s not just farming, it’s nice exercise for the body,” Pradhan says.

After they’ve tended to their crops, the women gather under a tree to share tea or a small picnic. This is their time to rest, tell jokes, play a game together on their phones, or talk about what’s on their minds. Pradhan’s day ends with more family time. She makes dinner for her family, and they tell each other about their day.

Saving time and money, improving crop yields

Pradhan began growing marigolds when the COVID-19 pandemic hit, to help support her family. She turned out to be a natural: Her first crop earned her a profit of 10,000 rupees (US$105), twice the average monthly salary for an Indian farmer. This success motivated her to add other flower varieties and to grow eggplants, cucumbers, and papayas to eat at home and to sell.

But before the hotline launched in 2022, every time Pradhan detected pests on her plants, she had to hire a rickshaw to get to the Block Agricultural Office and then wait all day to speak to someone. Not only was it time-consuming and costly, but any delay in visiting the office meant that the pests could spread and cause serious damage.

These trips also meant missing out on cherished afternoon hangouts with her female farmer friends. “We were losing that time and that happiness together,” she says.

All that changed with the introduction of the KSH hotline. And Pradhan has seen her crop yields improve thanks to the advice she’s received.

The free guidance from the hotline is one part of a holistic system developed by the Odisha state government with support from the Gates Foundation. The other part, Krushi Samiksha Kendra (KSK), is a centralized monitoring system—India’s first—that collects real-time data on conditions like pest incidence and extreme weather that affect the state’s more than 9 million farmers. The government relays this information to farmers via regular mobile alerts and voice messages, along with tips on accessing government support for buying seeds and other inputs.

Working and prospering together

Among all of the women in her village, Pradhan is especially close with Maharana, the president of the self-help group, whom she describes as a “sister.” They met about eight years ago, shortly after Maharana was widowed.

Together, they started farming some small patches of empty land, inspiring others to do the same. “When other women saw us two ladies working in the fields, it motivated them to join us,” Pradhan says. “We achieved a lot of things together. People started noticing us, and they started respecting us as well.”

As president and secretary of the self-help group, respectively, Maharana and Pradhan work with the other members to identify useful investments they can make as a group. For example, they pooled their resources to buy a machine that grinds grains and pulses into chhatua, a protein-rich powder that is mixed with milk or water to make a nutritious breakfast porridge. The members sell the powder at the market for extra income. The group has also invested in farming equipment—including a power tiller, a grass cutter, and an agricultural sprayer—to make their farming more efficient. When they are not using the equipment, they rent it out to other farmers and share the revenue.

The two leaders always consult each other and the other members when making decisions. “Even though Mrs. Maharana is the president of the group, she never makes a decision all on her own,” Pradhan says.

As secretary of the group, Pradhan manages the group’s finances, handles bank loans on its behalf, and organizes meetings and activities. She feels a deep responsibility to help individual group members whenever they have a problem, whether by lending them a small sum of money to get through hard times or helping with a family or personal issue.

Quicker answers, better harvests

Before the hotline started, Odisha’s farmers faced a range of challenges, from pests to cyclones and drought. Agricultural households in the state earned roughly 40% less than the national average. But since the launch of KSH and KSK, farmers who use the services have seen a 94% reduction in land affected by major pest outbreaks, resulting in as much as a 21% reduction in severe crop loss and more sustainable livelihoods. They get answers from the helpline within 48 hours, bringing agricultural expertise to even remote parts of the state that extension officers normally couldn’t reach. So far, at least 7.9 million farmers have benefited.

For Pradhan, these services have translated into higher yields, which means more time with the people she cares about—her family, Maharana, and her other friends in the self-help group. One of the group’s favorite activities is sewing school uniforms together for children in the village. Each year on November 14, Children’s Day in India, the group distributes uniforms to those who need them. “We feel so happy seeing these children wearing uniforms that were hand-stitched by us,” Pradhan says.

When technology can help farmers improve their agricultural practices, it also translates into more time with family and friends and a stronger and more resilient community. Pradhan no longer has to miss afternoon hangouts with her friends. “We have time to build relationships with each other and deepen our friendships,” she says. That’s what progress means for her.

item.title: Op vakantie met de kat Winnaarsverhalen 7 augustus 2026 Een feest voor vrienden en familie, én een vakantie waar zelfs de kat mee mag. In Blokker is de PostcodeStraatprijs gevallen op postcode 1695 HJ en dat zorgt voor veel blije gezichten. Lees meer
item.description:
Gaston deelt deze maand de PostcodeStraatprijs uit in Blokker, op postcode 1695 HJ. Daar vallen 10 winnaars in de prijzen. En hebben ze al plannen met hun prijs? Zeker! Van een groot feest tot een frisse airco tegen de hitte. Bij één van de winnaars mag zelfs de kat mee op vakantie.

vrijdag 7 augustus 2026 - Winnaarsverhalen

Een onvergetelijk feest 

Gerard en Matty winnen samen € 50.000,-. "We gaan een geweldig feest organiseren voor onze vrienden en familie", zegt Gerard blij. Bij Matty moet het besef nog indalen. "Echt onwerkelijk, dit", zegt ze. 

Een koele bestemming 

Met steeds hetere zomers in Nederland komt deze prijs precies op tijd: een airco. Zo blijft één winnaar straks lekker koel, wat de temperatuur ook doet. 

Op vakantie, met auto en al 

Ook een gloednieuwe BMW hoort bij de PostcodeStraatprijs. Alleen is de winnaar met vakantie als Gaston voor de deur staat. Samen met de buren belt hij het goede nieuws door. Bij thuiskomst staat de auto op hem te wachten.

item.title: Revised Arts & Culture Guidelines Emphasize Long-term Sustainability of New York’s Arts Community
item.description:
Photo courtesy of The Love Show.

Angela Harriell performing at The Love Show, a former Mrs. Fields Cookies store in Port Authority that has been transformed into a secret jewel box theater.

For over a decade, the Charles E. Culpeper Arts & Culture program goals and strategies have remained relatively consistent, providing clear long-term direction while allowing for refinement as the cultural landscape shifts. This spring, after a comprehensive review of grantmaking from 2021 to 2025, program staff made modest revisions to their guidelines to emphasize the long-term sustainability of the New York arts community alongside its vibrancy and inclusivity. The changes reflect increased investment in field building (including advocacy, field research, cross-sector collaborations, and cultural leadership development) and systemic solutions to ensure a thriving New York City creative sector over the long term.

The creative sector is essential infrastructure for civic engagement, economic opportunity, and community resilience. Artists play a vital role as truth-tellers, bridge-builders, and defenders of democratic values. Culpeper grantmaking between 2021 and 2025 prioritized diversity, accessibility, community engagement, and socially engaged practice. It supported creative work that might not otherwise have been realized, enriching the city’s vibrant landscape by challenging dominant narratives, creating space for alternative voices, and promoting greater understanding that can bring people together.

Through residencies and convenings across the city and at The Pocantico Center—where the 2022 opening of the David Rockefeller Creative Arts Center (DR Center) expanded year-round programming—Culpeper grantmaking also provided space and resources for creation and collaboration, increasingly scarce as costs outpaced artist incomes. As a result, grantee work reached new artists and audiences, contributing to New York City’s vitality as a cultural hub.

Photo Courtesy of Chashama.

A mural created by Bronx children during a Space to Create workshop led by Charles Esperanza.

Photo by Maria Baranova.

Joanna Kotze’s this is the beginning, this is the end 2026 Live Artery studio presentation. The show will premiere in November 2026.

Photo courtesy of Chashama. 

Jacob Lawrence weaves large-scale tapestries in his subsidized studio space at the Brooklyn Army Terminal.

Photo by Cherylynn Tsushima. 

The Chamber Music Society presented On Mars, performed by Jamie Barton, mezzo-soprano; Matthew Lipman, viola; and Tamar Sanikidze, piano.

Photo by Nir Arieli. 

Scene from an American Ballet Theater performance of Firebird.

The grantmaking review found durable gains over the last several years. Culpeper grants to major New York City museums have expand representation and chart paths for field-wide progress. Through sustained presentation of work by underrepresented artists and engagement with diverse local communities, institutions like the Queens Museum have come to function as civic infrastructure in neighborhoods under pressure from gentrification and displacement.  

A strengthened arts advocacy ecosystem has addressed immediate crises while building infrastructure for future generations. Serving as research partners, capacity builders, and advocacy coordinators, Culpeper grantee organizations helped advance New York City’s Cultural Plan, which has brought greater transparency and equity into the City’s cultural funding. Their efforts have expanded access to resources and fostered meaningful engagement between elected officials and cultural workers across all five boroughs.

Today, New York City’s creative sector faces an intensifying affordability crisis, funding instability, technological disruption, and attacks on diversity, equity, and inclusion initiatives in the aftermath of the COVID-19 pandemic that left deep marks on audience behavior and expectations. Economic insecurity is threatening the ability of organizations and artists to remain in the city; nearly 50 cultural venues have closed since the pandemic. The impacts fall hardest on organizations in lower-income communities, which often operate without the cushion of endowments or owned space. Federal retrenchment, including cuts from the National Endowment for the Arts, compounds the strain, as does a projected $8.8 billion city budget deficit in the coming years. Artificial intelligence is reshaping creative work, presenting new opportunities for innovation but also increasing employment risks.  

New York City’s creative sector stands at a critical juncture. After decades of growth that made it an economic engine and a defining feature of the city, challenges threaten the city’s standing as a global center for creativity. The Culpeper program’s emphasis on sustainability is more urgent than ever. The program will balance direct support for artists with investment in field-building strategies that provide long-term infrastructure for a thriving cultural community. And as the full scope of AI’s impact becomes evident, the program will also support exploratory work at the intersection of technology and the arts to encourage further learning and understanding.

New York City’s creative sector is not ancillary to civic life, but an essential component of a healthy democratic ecosystem. By elevating sustainability in its goal, the Culpeper program affirms its commitment to artists and to the conditions that allow them, and the city’s cultural life, to endure.

Angela Harriell performing at The Love Show, a former Mrs. Fields Cookies store in Port Authority that has been transformed into a secret jewel box theater.

For over a decade, the Charles E. The changes reflect increased investment in field building (including advocacy, field research, cross-sector collaborations, and cultural leadership development) and systemic solutions to ensure a thriving New York City creative sector over the long term.

Artists play a vital role as truth-tellers, bridge-builders, and defenders of democratic values. Culpeper grantmaking between 2021 and 2025 prioritized diversity, accessibility, community engagement, and socially engaged practice. It supported creative work that might not otherwise have been realized, enriching the city’s vibrant landscape by challenging dominant narratives, creating space for alternative voices, and promoting greater understanding that can bring people together.

Through residencies and convenings across the city and at The Pocantico Center—where the 2022 opening of the David Rockefeller Creative Arts Center (DR Center) expanded year-round programming—Culpeper grantmaking also provided space and resources for creation and collaboration, increasingly scarce as costs outpaced artist incomes. As a result, grantee work reached new artists and audiences, contributing to New York City’s vitality as a cultural hub.

item.title: Een hele bijzondere verjaardag Winnaarsverhalen 3 augustus 2026 Een verjaardag met een gouden randje én een auto als extra verrassing. In Sint-Oedenrode valt de PostcodeStraatprijs op postcode 5491 KS en dat maakt de dag voor de winnaars onvergetelijk. Lees meer
item.description:
Jarig zijn is al leuk, maar als Gaston langskomt met een gouden envelop wordt het extra feestelijk. 8 deelnemers in Sint-Oedenrode winnen € 25.000,- per lot. Op postcode 5491 KS is de PostcodeStraatprijs gevallen. Gaston Starreveld komt de winnaars verrassen. En hij heeft iets extra's bij zich: een taart voor de jarige job. 

maandag 3 augustus 2026 - Winnaarsverhalen

Verjaardagscadeau 

Yvette speelt mee met twee loten en wint € 50.000,-. Wat blijkt? Ze is vandaag ook jarig. "Wat een mooi cadeau is dit. Ik ben vanochtend al uitgebreid wezen shoppen met mijn dochter om het te vieren en dit maakt de dag nog mooier." 

Een auto én een vakantie 

Buurman Joan denkt rustig na over wat hij met zijn prijs gaat doen. "Ik denk dat het een vakantie wordt", zegt hij. Maar de dag wordt nog mooier voor Joan. Gaston haalt een autosleutel uit zijn zak en overhandigt hem. Joan valt eerst even stil. Zodra het besef landt, reageert hij: "Wow, dat is wel leuk!"

item.title: Help insecten de hitte door Goede doelen 3 augustus 2026 Bijen, vlinders en hommels hebben het zwaar wanneer het erg warm is. Door droogte vinden ze moeilijk water en nectar. En ze zoeken beschutte plekjes om uit te rusten. Goed nieuws: met een paar simpele tips help jij ze echt vooruit. Lees meer
item.description:
Bijen, vlinders en hommels hebben het zwaar wanneer het erg warm is. Door droogte vinden ze moeilijk water en nectar. En ze zoeken beschutte plekjes om uit te rusten. Goed nieuws: met een paar simpele tips help jij ze echt vooruit. 

maandag 3 augustus 2026 - Goede doelen

IVN Natuureducatie 

IVN Natuureducatie weet alles van dit soort problemen. Dit goede doel helpt mensen ontdekken hoe belangrijk natuur is en hoe je daarmee omgaat. Latifa Vonk van IVN Natuureducatie zegt het zo: "Insecten zijn onmisbaar voor onze natuur en ons voedsel. Met een paar simpele aanpassingen help je ze door de droge dagen." 

Tip 1: Waterschaaltjes in de schaduw 

Zet een schaaltje water neer op een schaduwplek in je tuin of op je balkon. Gooi er wat steentjes of knikkers in. Zo kunnen insecten ervan drinken zonder erin te vallen. Je zal zien dat zweefvliegen en bijen langskomen voor een slokje. Wespen nemen het water zelfs mee naar hun nest om dat af te koelen.

Tip 2: Water voor je planten

Planten die uitgedroogd zijn geven veel minder nectar. Dus geef je planten water, maar alleen als ze dat echt nodig hebben. Het beste is dat 's ochtends vroeg of 's avonds laat doen. Dan verdampt het niet meteen.

Slim idee: plaats een regenton. Zo vang je regenwater op en verspil je niet onnodig water. En je planten hebben minder water nodig als je de grond eromheen bedekt, bijvoorbeeld met bladeren of snoeiresten, mulchen noemen we dat. 

Tip 3: Bloeiende planten het hele jaar 

Plant later dit jaar onbespoten planten aan. Kies voor inheemse soorten die van nature in Nederland groeien. Zorg dat er het hele jaar door iets bloeit. Zo hebben insecten altijd voedsel. 

Samen impact maken

Dankzij jouw deelname kan de Postcode Loterij IVN Natuureducatie helpen. Dank daarvoor. En met deze tips kun je thuis ook aan de slag om de kleine beestjes te helpen. Zo maken we samen het verschil, ook tijdens de hete zomerdagen.

item.title: Global Gateway in the EU’s Enlargement and Eastern Neighbourhood regions
item.description:
What is Global Gateway

Global Gateway is the EU’s contribution to narrowing the global investment gap.  Over the period 2021-2024, €307 billion of investments have already been mobilised worldwide for sustainable and high-quality projects in the digital, climate, energy, health, transport and education sectors, taking into account the needs of partner countries and ensuring lasting benefits for local communities.

Global Gateway is implemented following a Team Europe approach, which brings together the EU and EU Member States (including their development finance institutions), as well as the European Investment Bank (EIB) and the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development (EBRD). Partner countries and the private sector are also key partners for Global Gateway implementation. The private sector has an essential role in bringing in investments and knowledge and in developing skills in partner countries.

Find general information about Global Gateway here.

Global Gateway in the EU’s Enlargement and Eastern Neighbourhood regions

In the EU’s Enlargement and Eastern Neighbourhood regions, Global Gateway investments contribute to 

  • connecting people and economies in the regions and with the EU. 
  • boosting growth potential and develop win-win supply chains
  • bridging the convergence gap and preparing the ground for future integration

These investments contribute to the reinforcement of our common prosperity, stability and security in the Enlargement and Eastern Neighbourhood regions.

Several strategies support the implementation of Global Gateway in the Enlargement and Eastern Neighbourhood regions:

  • Cross-Regional Connectivity Agenda
  • EU strategic approach to the Black Sea
  • Growth Plan for the Western Balkans
  • Moldova Growth Plan
  • Ukraine Facility

Financing Global Gateway

Financing tools such as the European Fund for Sustainable Development Plus (EFSD+) and its regional Investment Platforms, the Western Balkans Investment Framework and the Ukraine Investment Framework, all contribute to the implementation of Global Gateway.

Thanks to €13.23 billion provided by the EU budget from 2021 until May 2026, a total of €47.6 billion in investments are expected to be mobilised for the enlargement and Eastern Neighbourhood regions. Funding from other Team Europe Members comes on top of these amounts. 

This leverage is achieved with EU support provided in the form of budgetary guarantees, blending grants and also traditional grants to fund enabling projects.  In blending operations, EU grant funding is combined (“blended”) with loans from international financial institutions to make priority projects viable or to align a project with European standards. By reducing the risk for investors, budgetary guarantees, on the other hand, help to reduce the cost of financing for public and private investments.

ENEST Global Gateway Investment Hub

The ENEST Global Gateway Investment Hub aims to support and accelerate investments in in partner countries in the Enlargement and Eastern Neighbourhood Regions. It is coordinated by the European Commission’s Directorate General for Enlargement and Eastern Neighbourhood. 

The Investment Hub connects European companies, EU Member States and financial institutions, and can involve partner country companies and authorities, to mobilise financial and non-financial support under the Global Gateway strategy. 

As part of the ENEST Global Gateway Investment Hub, the European Commission regularly opens calls for expressions of interest for private investments in specific enlargement and Eastern Neighbourhood countries. 

ENEST Global Gateway Investment Hub

Selected ongoing projects

Trans-Balkan Electricity Corridor 

Installation of overhead transmission lines, building of new substations and upgrading of existing ones in the 488 km Trans-Balkan Power Corridor which connects the electricity transmission systems in Serbia, Montenegro and Bosnia and Herzegovina with the systems in Croatia, Hungary, Romania and Italy. 

Link to project fiche

WiFi for Western Balkans

Providing total funding for free high-speed Wi-Fi connection to public buildings, urban public spaces and rural areas in up to 500 municipalities in the Western Balkans, bringing connectivity closer to citizens and allowing them to benefit from the opportunities of digitalisation. 

Link to project fiche

Education infrastructure improvement in Montenegro 

Construction and renovation of kindergartens, primary, secondary and vocational schools as well as providing IT equipment for educational facilities in Podgorica and nine other municipalities in Montenegro.  

Link to project fiche

Railway line Uzhhorod-Chop in Ukraine

Within the EU’s Solidarity Lanes initiative, this project built a railway line with the standard EU track width of a 1,435 mm gauge to connect the cities of Uzhhorod and Chop and onwards to the EU. 

Link to project fiche

Bălți regional hospital in Moldova

Constructing and equipping a regional tertiary care hospital with a capacity of 340 hospital beds and 78 beds in the ambulatory services, on a built surface of 38,000 m2, in the Northern part of Moldova. 

Link to project fiche

EU4Business in the Eastern Neighbourhood

Support to private sector development by improving access to finance for SMEs, promoting better business regulations facilitating access to business development services and helping SMEs take advantage of present and future trade opportunities. 

Link to project fiche

Click on the map for more project examples 

Global Gateway in your country

Select a region for more information

Western Balkans

In the framework of Global Gateway, the EU’s investments aim to support a green and digital transition and bring the Western Balkans region closer to the EU’s single market. Since 2021 the EU has already mobilised an expected €1.5 billion in investments thanks to €588 million in EU and Bilateral Donor grants. Funds are raised through tools such as the Western Balkans Investment Framework (WBIF).

Project examples

Floating Solar Photovoltaic Power Plant in Vau i Dejës lake

Tirana by-pass: Blue Highway

Durres-Tirana railway line

Rail interconnection Vorë-Hani i Hotit section

Belshi solar photovoltaic power plant

Establishment of smart labs - network of ICT labs in the pre-university education system

In the framework of Global Gateway, the EU’s investments aim to support a green and digital transition and bring the Western Balkans region closer to the EU’s single market. For projects in Bosnia and Herzegovina, since 2021 the EU has mobilised €2.7 billion in investments thanks to €1.1 billion in EU and Bilateral Donor grants. Funds are raised through tools such as the Western Balkans Investment Framework (WBIF).

Project examples

Road Corridor Vc

Reconstruction and modernisation of Brčko river port

Sarajevo Water project: reconstruction of water supply network

In the framework of Global Gateway, the EU has identified investment priorities to spur long-term growth, accelerate the green and digital transition, and foster regional cooperation. For projects in Kosovo, since 2021, the EU has already mobilised €774 million in investments thanks to €240 million in EU funding. Funds are raised through tools such as the Western Balkans Investment Framework (WBIF).

Project examples

Support to waste management

Solar for Kosovo II - district heating

Wastewater treatment in Mitrovica

In the framework of Global Gateway, the EU’s investments aim to support a green and digital transition and bring the Western Balkans region closer to the EU’s single market. For projects in Montenegro, since 2021 the EU has mobilised €1.3 billion in investments thanks to €429 million in EU and Bilateral Donor grants. Funds are raised through tools such as the Western Balkans Investment Framework (WBIF).

Project examples

Rail Route 4 - Bar-Vrbnica railway line section

Podgorica wastewater treatment plant

Municipal water and sanitation infrastructure

Education infrastructure improvement

In the framework of Global Gateway, the EU’s investments aim to support a green and digital transition and bring the Western Balkans region closer to the EU’s single market. For projects in North Macedonia, since 2021 the EU has mobilised €1.9 billion in investments thanks to €676 million in EU and Bilateral Donor grants. Funds are raised through tools such as the Western Balkans Investment Framework (WBIF).

Project examples

Rail interconnection North Macedonia-Bulgaria

Bogdanci Wind Park

Oslomej 1 solar photovoltaic power plant

Skopje wastewater treatment plant

In the framework of Global Gateway, the EU’s investments aim to support a green and digital transition and bring the Western Balkans region closer to the EU’s single market. For projects in Serbia, since 2021 the EU has mobilised €8.1 billion in investments thanks to €1.8 billion in EU and Bilateral Donor grants. Funds are raised through tools such as the Western Balkans Investment Framework (WBIF).

Project examples

University Children's Hospital Tiršova 2

Rail Corridor X

Rhine-Danube Corridor- facilitating navigation in the Prahovo sector

Kostolac wind farm

Gas interconnector Serbia-Bulgaria

Regional programmes across the Western Balkan region support key investments in transport, energy, digital connections and human capital development. Since 2021 the EU has mobilised €4.3 billion in investments thanks to €1.3 billion in EU funding. Funds are raised through tools such as the Western Balkans Investment Framework (WBIF).

Project examples

Trans-Balkan Electricity Corridor

Wi-Fi for Western Balkans

Regional Energy Efficiency Programme

Go Digital in the Western Balkans

Unlocking private investments in the Western Balkans

Türkiye

The Turkey Investment Platform is the main vehicle to channel EU investments in Türkiye. The Platform supports investment proposals by the EU and European and international financial institutions in the areas of decarbonisation, digitalisation, access to finance, innovation, and green investments, through a wide range of budgetary guarantee mechanisms for public and private investments. Under EFSD+ Private Sector Investment guarantees (Open Architecture), a total of 14 guarantees have Türkiye as an eligible country. Since the establishment of the Turkey Investment Platform in 2022, the EU has mobilised € 2.1 billion in investments thanks to almost €70 million from EU funding.

Project examples

Construction of Çerkezköy-Kapıkule railway section

Research on rare earth elements

Improved access to water and water networks

Eastern Neighbourhood

Through Global Gateway the EU has been supporting access to finance for small and medium-sized businesses, energy efficiency solutions, the rehabilitation of education infrastructure and improved water management, among other sectors. Expected mobilised investments since 2021 now exceed €2.7 billion, thanks to €185 million in EU funding.

Project examples

Resilient Syunik Team Europe Initiative

Sisian-Kajaran Road

Syunik Customs and Logistics Centre

Yerevan Customs and Logistics Centre

Caucasus Transmission Network

Under the Global Gateway strategy, expected mobilised investments now exceed €130 million, fostering the country’s economic diversification, accelerating the green and digital transition, and promoting smarter and greener cities.

Project examples

Ganja street lighting

Ganja water and wastewater networks

Nakhchivan railway feasibility study

Greening the Port of Baku

Global Gateway supports investments and mobilises the private sector and international financing institutions, towards more resilient economies. It delivers concrete benefits for people in areas such as transport, energy, environment and climate, water and sanitation and digital development. Since 2021 the EU has already mobilised an expected €2.8 billion in investments thanks to €541 million in EU and Bilateral Donor grants.

Project examples

Balti regional hospital

Energy efficiency in healthcare and educational institutions

Moldova roads rehabilitation V

Termoelectrica - Chisinau district heating

Moldova-Romania power interconnection

North-South railway corridor

Startup City Cahul

Global Gateway supports investments and mobilises the private sector and international financing institutions towards more resilient economies. It delivers concrete benefits for people in areas such as transport, energy, environment and climate, water and sanitation and digital development. Since 2021 the EU has already mobilised an expected €12.3 billion in investments thanks to €4.1billion in EU and Bilateral Donor grants.

Project examples

Upgrading border crossing points

Railway line Uzhhorod-Chop

Ukrenergo power transmission

Energy efficiency and emergency repairs

Regional programmes across the Eastern Neighbourhood region support key investments in energy, digital connections, transport, environment and human capital development. Since 2021 the EU has mobilised €1.4 billion in investments thanks to €338 million in EU funding.

Project examples

EU4Business

EU4Digital

EaPConnect

EU4Environment

Black Sea submarine digital cable

Black Sea submarine electricity cable

Global Gateway Flagship Projects

Global Gateway flagship projects are priority projects jointly identified by Team Europe actors and partners. An overview of flagship projects can be found here 

Global Gateway flagship projects in the Western Balkans and Türkiye 

Global Gateway flagship projects in the Eastern Neighbourhood

item.title: Agradecimento ao BPI Fundação La Caixa
item.description:
A Fundação Bissaya Barreto agradece ao BPI e à Fundação “la Caixa” o apoio atribuído no âmbito da sua Iniciativa Social Descentralizada.

Através desta iniciativa solidária, a Fundação Bissaya Barreto recebeu um apoio financeiro de dez mil euros para o projeto de recuperação de danos provocados pela tempestade Kristin em alguns dos seus estabelecimentos e equipamentos sociais e educativos localizados em Coimbra, Figueira da Foz e Monte Redondo.

Este contributo representou uma ajuda fundamental para a reposição das condições necessárias ao desenvolvimento da nossa missão, permitindo dar continuidade ao trabalho que realizamos diariamente em prol da comunidade.

Em nome dos utentes e famílias que beneficiam da nossa atividade, agradecemos ao BPI e à Fundação “la Caixa” a confiança depositada e o compromisso demonstrado com as instituições sociais e com as comunidades afetadas por situações adversas.

The post Agradecimento ao BPI Fundação La Caixa appeared first on Fundação Bissaya Barreto.

item.title: De familie opzoeken in een nieuwe BMW Winnaarsverhalen 31 juli 2026 Goed nieuws in Zaandam. Op postcode 1502 VP valt de PostcodeStraatprijs. 6 deelnemers winnen elk € 25.000,- per lot. Lees meer
item.description:
Goed nieuws in Zaandam. Op postcode 1502 VP valt de PostcodeStraatprijs. 6 deelnemers winnen elk € 25.000,- per lot. En als kers op de taart mag Gaston ook nog iemand blij maken met een gloednieuwe BMW.

vrijdag 31 juli 2026 - Winnaarsverhalen

Samen een eigen bedrijf 

Gaston bezoekt Agate en Demian. Het stel heeft een eigen bedrijf. "We willen daar graag verder in investeren", zegt Demian. De prijs is meer dan welkom. "Dit is echt geweldig!" 

Comfortabel op weg 

Gaston heeft nog een verrassing voor Agate en Demian: ze winnen ook de BMW! Het stel rijdt elk jaar naar familie in Polen, in een auto die zijn beste tijd wel heeft gehad. Agate en Demian kunnen het bijna niet geloven. "Wauw, dat meen je niet!" 

53 jaar samen, en nu dit 

Bij Wim en Joke ligt het net ontvangen Postcode Loterij zomercadeau nog op tafel. "Altijd leuk om wat cadeau te krijgen", zegt Wim. Dan haalt Gaston de gouden envelop tevoorschijn. Joke ziet het bedrag en haar ogen worden groot. "Zo hé, dit komt even binnen", zegt ze met tranen van vreugde. Wim slaat zijn armen om haar heen. "We gaan onze kleinkinderen heel blij maken."

item.title: Trust for Civic Life Awards $7.6 million to 20 New Civic Hubs
item.description:
2026 Civic Hub grantee Protect the Sacred works across the Navajo Nation in rural New Mexico, creating culturally grounded pathways for rural Diné (Navajo) communities to strengthen community participation, preserve Indigenous knowledge, and shape community-led solutions. Photo courtesy of Protect the Sacred.

The following is an excerpt from the Trust for Civic Life.

The Trust for Civic Life has awarded $7.6 million to 20 new Civic Hub grantees, local groups across rural America working to rebuild trust and connection outside of politics. It’s the Trust’s third round of grants as a philanthropic collaborative that brings together national funders of various backgrounds and ideologies to invest in locally led civic efforts as a strategy for addressing the country’s deep divides.

Since the Trust launched in 2024, it has invested nearly $27 million into rural regions, which receive just 3 percent of national philanthropic funding. The new funding follows the Trust’s latest survey of more than 1,000 rural community members, which found that trust in national institutions is eroding but trust, agency, and belonging all remain strong locally, and are closely tied to neighbors taking action together.

“Americans are telling us that national politics are leaving them frustrated and without agency, but they still feel connected to their own communities and believe they can effect change where they live and work,” said Charlie Brown, Executive Director of the Trust for Civic Life. “That’s a powerful insight, and we see it reflected in the work of each of our new Civic Hub grantees.” 

Continue reading at the Trust for Civic Life.

The Trust for Civic Life is a grantmaking collaborative supporting the community efforts that help Americans connect, solve problems together, and feel confident in a shared future. Launched in 2024, the collaborative brings together a cross-ideological team of funders to invest $50 million by 2028 in a new wave of local civic opportunities that increase trust, agency, and belonging in rural America. Through its grantmaking, the Trust funds both the critical groundwork and promising experiments that allow civic participation to take hold in rural communities and spread across the country. The Trust was initiated by the Rockefeller Brothers Fund, Stand Together, and Omidyar Network, and has grown to include 23 funding members from national philanthropy and the private sector.

item.title: Help de dieren in de hitte Goede doelen 30 juli 2026 Hoge temperaturen zijn niet alleen voor mensen zwaar. Ook huisdieren kunnen last krijgen van de hitte. Met deze tips van de Dierenbescherming help jij je dier koel en comfortabel de zomer door. Lees meer
item.description:
Stijgt de temperatuur buiten? Dan is het extra belangrijk om op je huisdier te letten. Dieren kunnen namelijk niet goed tegen warmte. Oververhitting kan gevaarlijk zijn, en soms zelfs dodelijk. Maar hoe merk je dat je huisdier het te warm heeft? En hoe koel je hem weer af? 

donderdag 30 juli 2026 - Goede doelen

De Dierenbescherming 

De Dierenbescherming geeft antwoord. Zij komen dagelijks in actie voor dieren in nood, ook als het gaat om hitte. Hieronder lees je hoe jij zelf in actie komt voor huisdieren tijdens hete dagen. 
 

Hoe merk je dat een dier het te warm heeft? 

De slijmvliezen zijn rood. Het dier voelt heet aan, ademt snel, wil niet eten en is lusteloos. Honden kunnen gaan braken. Vogels zitten vaak met hun veren gespreid en hun snavel open. 

Hoe herken je een hitteshock bij huisdieren? 

Wordt de oververhitting te erg? Dan kan je dier een hitteshock krijgen. Je herkent dit aan een snelle hartslag en ademhaling. Ook reageert je dier niet of nauwelijks meer op prikkels. Bel in dat geval direct de dierenarts en begin met koelen. 

Hoe koel je je huisdier af? 

Breng je dier naar een koele plek en zorg voor vers drinkwater. Honden, katten, konijnen en knaagdieren kun je nat maken. Doe dat vooral bij de kop, oren, hals en poten. Gebruik geen ijskoud water. Daardoor trekken bloedvaten samen, en dat maakt het juist moeilijker voor je huisdier om warmte kwijt te raken. 
 

Hond laten zwemmen? 

Heb je een hond die van water houdt? Laat hem lekker zwemmen of pootjebaden. Laat hem daarna niet opdrogen in de volle zon. Let op: te veel water binnenkrijgen kan gevaarlijk zijn en leiden tot watervergiftiging. Pas ook op voor blauwalg. 

Jouw deelname telt 

Dankzij jouw deelname kan de Postcode Loterij de Dierenbescherming steunen. Heel erg bedankt daarvoor. Ook namens de Dierenbescherming.

item.title: The West Advances Solutions to Lower Costs With More Clean Energy
item.description:
The goal of the Foundation’s Climate and Clean Energy program is to protect people and the planet from the worst impacts of climate change by helping make energy clean, affordable, safe, and reliable for all. We support organizations, projects, and coalitions that help advance and implement policies to accelerate progress on clean energy, which can provide affordable and reliable energy for households and communities. Read the full story below.

Energy Affordability

“This is really a moment for states to do everything they can to address affordability."

Leah Rubin Shen, managing director of the western region, Advanced Energy Institute

Leah Rubin Shen has seen the cost of clean energy—think solar, wind, and battery storage—drop over the course of her more than 10-year career. These days, the price of clean energy isn’t the problem. Indeed, affordability is its selling point, and affordability is top of mind for many these days. 

Electricity bills in the U.S. increased an average of $110 per household between 2024 and 2025. Grid repairs due to aging infrastructure and extreme weather, combined with more natural gas price volatility due to wars in Iran and Ukraine, are the main drivers of electricity cost increases. 

“This is really a moment for states to do everything they can to address affordability,” said Rubin Shen, western regional managing director for Advanced Energy Institute, an association dedicated to clean energy and electrification.

Aerial view of a solar panel array in rural Oregon overlooking a valley, and powerlines outside Las Vegas, Nevada.

One straightforward way for states to manage rising energy costs is to invest in more clean energy. Once a clean energy project is built, operating costs are very low. This stands in stark contrast to natural gas power plants, which are prone to sudden price increases.

“Renewables, by definition, don’t have a fuel cost,” said Michael Colvin, director of Environmental Defense Fund’s California clean energy program. “If you have an economy that’s more dependent on renewable resources, you’re more immune to those price shocks.” 

In addition, the cost of building clean energy projects has been coming down fast. More than 90 percent of new renewable energy projects in 2024 cost less and were quicker to build than fossil fuel alternatives. Clean energy is also key to helping fight climate change. Unlike natural gas and coal plants, solar and wind power plants don’t release air pollution.  

Notably, clean energy progress is accelerating across the country as states race to satisfy growing energy demands—and not just in places with a reputation for climate leadership. Texas now leads the nation in wind energy production with Iowa, Oklahoma, and Kansas close behind. Indiana, Kentucky, and Utah saw the largest amount of clean energy growth in the last year.

“Cheap, clean electricity is important for meeting rising energy demand as well as helping society switch from fossil fuels to electricity to power transportation and heat buildings,” said Laura Wisland, deputy director of the Heising-Simons Foundation’s Climate and Clean Energy Program. 

California Blazing a Clean Energy Trail

"We borrowed all the good ideas and iterated on them. All of the activity that the West is going to do into electricity markets over the next two years is going to define the next decade"

Michael Colvin, director of the Environmental Defense Fund’s California clean energy program

California has been a clean energy leader for decades, and in 2025, it took a significant step toward making it easier for states throughout the West to invest in clean energy and lower energy costs for millions of consumers. Thanks to support from the Heising-Simons Foundation, clean energy advocates helped the state work with its western neighbors to lay the foundation for a larger, more integrated energy market that will allow electricity to be traded more efficiently across the West. The enhanced coordination enabled by the new market will allow states to invest in more clean energy and eliminate redundant investments needed to keep power supplies reliable. This will save energy customers billions of dollars.   

Energy markets can be wonky and complex, but the Heising-Simons Foundation understands the value of investing in organizations focused on the technicalities. The details matter.

“There’s only a handful of funders that are deep enough in the details to understand what’s going on,” Rubin Shen said. “Heising-Simons is one of those.”

The new western market will be governed by an independent nonprofit called the Regional Organization for Western Energy (ROWE). The ROWE was born out of a multi-stakeholder collaborative that formed years ago when several western states realized that by working together, they could save electricity customers money and improve grid reliability. The collaborative was comprised of a variety of stakeholders, including consumer advocates, utilities, clean energy advocates, technology providers, and several Heising-Simons Foundation grantee partners. The stakeholders looked at other organized energy markets for inspiration, explained Colvin, who sits on the Pathways Initiative Launch Committee, which advises the ROWE as it starts up.

“We borrowed all the good ideas and iterated on them,” he said. “All of the activity that the West is going to do into electricity markets over the next two years is going to define the next decade,” Colvin said. “This is an absolute inflection point for all customers.”

In fact, the ROWE is integrating customer protections into its backbone. The organization’s bylaws specifically call out protecting the public interest. The ROWE must establish an Office of Public Participation, something no other regional energy market has accomplished, said Kelsie Gomanie, the western markets advocate for the Natural Resources Defense Council’s Sustainable FERC Project team.

“This will be totally novel to an electricity market governance framework,” she said. “The ROWE may even help push eastern regional trade organizations to recognize that transparency helps them be more successful. It’s really the highest tier of inclusive governance.” 

Photos: Turbines in Altamont Pass Wind Farm near Livermore, California, and solar panels on the roof of downtown Sacramento’s Golden 1 Center – home of the Sacramento Kings NBA team.

The Future Looks Bright in the West, with Promising Outlooks Elsewhere too

"What's happening in the West right now is the result of years of painstaking, unglamorous work — states sitting across from each other, stakeholders setting aside their differences, and advocates refusing to give up on a vision that many said was impossible."

Laura Wisland, Deputy Director, Climate and Clean Energy Program, Heising-Simons Foundation

Since the U.S. Congress rescinded major federal support for wind and solar last year, clean energy advocates have shifted their focus to opportunities at the state and local levels. The creation of the ROWE—and what it will deliver in terms of climate benefits and cheaper electricity prices—is a bright spot in an otherwise challenging environment for clean energy progress.

“What’s happening in the West right now is the result of years of painstaking, unglamorous work: states sitting across from each other, stakeholders setting aside their differences, and advocates refusing to give up on a vision that many said was impossible,” explained Wisland. “The creation of the ROWE is proof that persistence pays off. Western states will have a truly independent, home-grown market that stitches together the region’s extraordinary clean energy resources—sun, wind, geothermal—and delivers the benefits to families and businesses. It’s a solution built by the West, for the West. And when it’s fully running, it will mean cheaper, cleaner, more reliable electricity for millions of people, and real money in people’s pockets.”

The post The West Advances Solutions to Lower Costs With More Clean Energy appeared first on Heising-Simons Foundation.

item.title: Volop mooie plannen in Vught Winnaarsverhalen 27 juli 2026 Trouwfeesten, nieuwe fietsen en een dak dat eindelijk gerepareerd wordt. In Vught barst het los aan plannen, want de PostcodeStraatprijs is gevallen op postcode 5262 XC. Lees meer
item.description:
Trouwfeesten, nieuwe fietsen en een dak dat eindelijk gerepareerd wordt. In Vught barst het los aan plannen, want de PostcodeStraatprijs is gevallen op postcode 5262 XC. 

maandag 27 juli 2026 - Winnaarsverhalen

Reis moet nog even wachten 

Winnaar Jacky droomt van Indonesië. Maar die reis moet nog een jaartje wachten: ze wordt namelijk oma. "En dat heb ik er graag voor over", lacht ze. 

Een tafel en een dak 

Bij Hugo en Anne is het huis al aardig vol. Ze hebben een dochter van anderhalf en de tweede is op komst. Anne wil een nieuwe eettafel met mooie stoelen. Hugo denkt liever aan het dak, dat aan vernieuwing toe is. Maar zodra hij het bedrag ziet, is hij om. "Er mag sowieso een nieuwe eettafel worden aangeschaft, haha!" 

Dubbel feest 

Voor Margo en Ronald is het dubbel feest. Naast € 25.000,- per lot winnen zij ook een gloednieuwe BMW. Gaston haalt de autosleutel tevoorschijn. Margo slaat haar hand voor haar mond. "Wauw, dit is echt ongelooflijk!", reageert Ronald.
